When you call something exemplary, you are saying it is so outstandingly good that it works as a model — a shining example that other people should look up to and try to copy. It is not just "good" or even "very good." It sits at a level where you point to it and say, "This is what it should look like. Everyone else, take note."

Think of it this way: if a student gets an A+, you might say they did "excellent" work. But if a teacher holds up that student's essay in front of the class and says, "This is how an essay should be written — study this," that essay has now become exemplary. The difference is that exemplary work doesn't just succeed — it sets the standard.
The two senses of the word

Exemplary has two related but distinct uses.

1. A model of excellence (the most common meaning)

This is how you will encounter the word 99% of the time. It describes something — a person's behavior, their work, their character — that is so commendably high in quality that it acts as a benchmark for others.

  • An employee who always shows up on time, treats colleagues with respect, meets every deadline, and goes beyond what is asked of them would be described as having exemplary conduct.
  • A nurse who is patient, precise, compassionate, and never makes an error would be giving exemplary care.
  • A leader who makes fair decisions, stays calm under pressure, and inspires their team would be an exemplary leader.

In all of these cases, the message is the same: this person or thing represents the ideal standard — the version others should aspire to.

2. A warning example (formal and less common)

Less commonly, particularly in legal and formal contexts, exemplary is used to mean "serving as a harsh warning to others." This is where the word takes a slightly different angle: instead of being an example of what to do, it becomes an example of what happens when you do wrong.

  • Exemplary punishment means a punishment so severe that it is meant to frighten others out of committing the same act.
  • Exemplary damages is a legal term where a court awards extra money — beyond what covers actual losses — specifically to make a public example of the wrongdoer and deter others.

Even here, the root idea is the same: making an example. Whether positive or negative, something exemplary is held up as a reference point for everyone else.

Very strong. Exemplary carries a sense of admiration and high praise. It implies that someone has not just done their job or met expectations — they have exceeded them in a way that stands apart from the crowd. When you use this word to describe a person, it is one of the highest compliments you can give them.

Consider the difference in weight between these sentences:

  • "She is a good doctor." — She does her job well.
  • "She is an excellent doctor." — She performs at a high level.
  • "She is an exemplary doctor." — She represents what every doctor should be.

That last sentence carries not just praise, but a sense of standard-setting.

• It does not simply mean "good" or "impressive." Those words don't carry the implication of being a model for others.
  • It is not the same as "perfect." Something can be exemplary without being flawless — it just needs to be good enough that it becomes the reference point others look to.
  • It is not a neutral word. It almost always carries positive admiration (in its common sense), or deliberate severity (in its legal/warning sense).

You will most often see exemplary paired with words like:

  • exemplary behavior / conduct — acting in a way that others should imitate
  • exemplary work / performance — producing results that set the benchmark
  • exemplary service — serving people at the highest possible standard
  • exemplary student / employee / citizen — a person who embodies the ideal of their role
  • exemplary punishment / damages — a consequence designed to make a public example
The single sentence to remember it by

Exemplary means so outstandingly good that it becomes the example everyone else should follow — or, in formal/legal use, so deliberately severe that it warns others not to follow the same wrong path.

If you can remember that this word always involves making an example — whether of excellence or of consequence — you will always use and understand it correctly.
